summary.text: 坏 has two distinct roles: it is an older graph attested for a mound and glossed as unbaked tile, and it is the modern simplified spelling of 壞, meaning “bad” or “ruined.” The older word written 坏 may have sounded like the word written 壞, prompting the spelling reuse, but its pronunciation is not supplied.

formation.text: The older graph 坏 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 土 contributes an earth-related category, and 不 is identified as a sound element. This construction belongs to the older graph; the modern use of 坏 for 壞 is a separate spelling function.

components.text: 土 contributes an earth-related category in the historical analysis, consistent with the recorded mound and unbaked-tile uses.
不 is named as the sound element in the historical analysis. Its modern Mandarin reading can be compared with 坏’s, but that present-day comparison does not establish their historical sound relation.

history.text: Historical accounts distinguish 坏, analyzed as 土 plus 不, from 壞, analyzed as 土 plus 褱. The glosses for 坏 include a mound and unbaked tile, but do not establish which sense came first.
A cited bronze inscription uses 坏 for a mound. Other references record unbaked-material senses for 坯 or related 坏 forms; they do not establish an order between these uses.
Warring States and Qin manuscript contexts use 壞 for ruin or damage. A Qin bronze also uses 壞 to spell a place name read as 褱德, a separate use from the ruin sense.

A modern standard table maps 坏 to 壞 as its simplified form. The graph may have been reused because the older word written 坏 sounded like the word written 壞; the older word’s pronunciation and the start of this spelling use remain unresolved.
Descriptions record bronze and manuscript examples for 壞 and forms from later script periods, but do not settle the absolute earliest attestation of either graph.

uncertainties.text: The mound and unbaked-tile uses of historical 坏 have no established chronology connecting them to each other, to 壞’s ruin senses, or to 坏’s modern spelling use.

The proposed sound-based explanation for 坏’s modern spelling of 壞 cannot be confirmed because the older mound or pottery word’s pronunciation is not supplied.
